source.title: AdaSAM: Boosting Sharpness-Aware Minimization with Adaptive Learning Rate and Momentum for Training Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Hao Sun; Li Shen; Qi-Huang Zhong; Liang Ding; Shi-Xiang Chen; Jing-Wei Sun; Jing Li; Guang-Zhong Sun; Da-Cheng Tao

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present. Some equations and table layouts are flattened, but the optimizer comparison tables are recoverable.
record.tranche_reason: Compares adaptive optimizers with SGD and SAM on held-out GLUE task metrics, using a different model and benchmark from the claim’s cited comparisons.
record.gate_note: The study reports held-out benchmark metrics for optimizer comparisons. Its batch-size experiment reports training-loss curves and speed, not held-out performance; sharpness is discussed but not measured. Cited prior work is not extracted as a result.
record.test_reason: AMSGrad versus SGD provides a direct adaptive-versus-nonadaptive held-out performance comparison in a new setting: pretrained RoBERTa-large fine-tuning on GLUE. The experiment does not establish comparable optimizer tuning or training performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: they establish an O(1/√(bT)) stationarity convergence rate under assumptions and report superior selected AdaSAM performance on GLUE. Their empirical superiority claim is aggregate and task-dependent, rather than a win on every task or metric.
record.recipe_differences: Compares AdaSAM, AMSGrad, SAM, and SGD while fine-tuning RoBERTa-large on GLUE; the claim’s optimizer version concerns adaptive methods’ held-out performance under limited tuning. This study tests a related optimizer comparison, not the claim’s cited recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and optimizer choice; neighborhood size ρ; momentum setting β1 = 0.9 versus β1 = 0.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing AdaSAM batch size from 4 to 32 with square-root learning-rate scaling accelerates training-loss reduction on MRPC, RTE, and CoLA; the theorem bounds convergence toward stationarity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: AdaSAM can achieve mini-batch speedup in optimization under the stated assumptions and learning-rate scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: AdaSAM's selected aggregate GLUE score exceeds AMSGrad's, but this measures the proposed sharpness-aware optimizer's performance rather than a sharpness–generalization-gap correlation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding the tested SAM perturbation to AMSGrad can improve selected GLUE fine-tuning scores.

record.code_released: https://github.com/facebookresearch/fairseq (toolkit URL stated; study code release not stated)
record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the task metrics. It says hyperparameters include learning rate, epochs, and batch size, but detailed settings are deferred to an appendix; the supplied text does not describe broad tuning or matched training performance for the optimizer comparison.
record.rows_left_out: Table I reports additional individual task metrics for SAM, AdaSAM variants, and AdaSAM(best); these are not extracted because the kept rows cover the adaptive-versus-SGD comparison and its aggregate result. Table II reports the β1 = 0 ablation and is omitted to stay within the row cap; it also compares adaptive methods with SGD and reports an aggregate AdaSAM(best) score of 89.52 versus SGD 37.23 and AMSGrad 88.79.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its contrast with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.

Image classification, word-level language modeling, Adam itself, comparable optimized training performance, a documented learning-rate and decay tuning comparison, broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, and switching optimizers.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and remedies for a large-batch penalty.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on data size or augmentation.
Measured magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap correlations, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Removal of highly memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Table III supplies task-level learning rates, batches, update budgets, and warmup settings, but no optimizer-specific tuning search. Figures 1 and 3 and the accompanying text describe slower loss reduction for SGD, so the comparison does not isolate a generalization gap at matched training fit. Table II's no-momentum results are already declared in rows_left_out and therefore are not missing. Lack of uncertainty alone does not justify a limits_scope verdict for AdaSAM. V4 says adaptive methods often perform worse, not always; this new-setting reversal qualifies its scope rather than refuting the overall frequency claim.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization are not tested.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.

Tests RoBERTa-large fine-tuning on GLUE with AMSGrad, SGD, SAM, and AdaSAM; does not test Adam, language-model pretraining, the cited benchmarks, broad hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, or switching optimizers.
Batch-size results concern training loss and convergence speed, not held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
No trained-network sharpness measurement or comparison with other generalization measures.

relationships.condition: AMSGrad versus momentum SGD, RoBERTa-large fine-tuning on eight GLUE tasks, β1 = 0.9, using the reported training settings
relationships.reason: R1–R10 show AMSGrad exceeding SGD on every reported metric, with reported averages 89.52 versus 55.8; this identifies a reverse-ordering setting, while undocumented optimizer-specific tuning and unequal convergence prevent attributing it to generalization at comparable training performance.
relationships.display_finding: AMSGrad reportedly outperformed SGD across all reported metrics, but these comparisons remain unverified. Differences in how fully the methods converged make it harder to tell whether their performance gap reflects how well they generalize.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: AMSGrad versus SGD across the 8 reported GLUE tasks, β1 = 0.9
reader_labels.reason: AMSGrad scores higher than SGD on all reported task metrics and has a higher aggregate average (R1–R10). This is evidence against adaptive optimizers always generalizing worse in this tested setting.

reader_labels.reason: AdaSAM has a higher reported aggregate average than both comparators, but the paper does not report an aggregate uncertainty estimate or broad optimizer tuning (R10–R11).
